notes:
**2 Corinthians 12: verse-by-verse research notes**

Gaps first: I ran out of search and fetch calls before I could check netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org (Chrysostom), oca.org, the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org) or ag.org. I also found nothing on word-of-faith or prosperity readings of the thorn, because that search didn't run. The Enduring Word page cut off partway through v. 8, so for vv. 9–21 the main source is Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) on StudyLight.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik says the "super apostles" in Corinth probably claimed spectacular visions. Paul has been boasting reluctantly since chapter 11 and now boasts of his own visions, but he is tired of talking about himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-12/
- JFB: "visions" are things seen and "revelations" are things heard or revealed. Paul tells the story to show the weakness that followed the vision, not his own glory. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik: Paul writes in the third person so he won't glorify himself. The switch to "I" in v. 7 shows he means himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-12/
- JFB dates the vision to about AD 41–43, roughly when Paul visited Jerusalem in Acts 22:17. Paul knew the Corinthians for years and never mentioned it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html
- "Third heaven": Guzik says this doesn't mean levels of heaven. It was common language: sky, then stars, then the place where God reigns. JFB gives the same three-part scheme. (Same two URLs.)

**v. 3**
- Guzik: Paul repeats "in the body or out of it" twice. If Paul didn't know, we can't, so guessing is pointless. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-12/
- JFB: Paul accepts that a spirit without a body can still be aware of things. Not knowing *how* it happened doesn't cancel the fact that it did. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik: "Paradise" comes from a Persian word for a royal walled garden. Paul says nothing of what he saw and only hints at what he heard. Contrast that with today's breathless reports of heavenly visits. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-12/
- JFB: the words weren't impossible to say in themselves. They were meant to comfort Paul personally, not to be passed on. JFB, following Bengel, treats Paradise as an inner part of the third heaven. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html

**vv. 5–6**
- Guzik: Paul won't play the fool like the super-apostles, but he lets the Corinthians know he really did have such experiences. He wants to be judged by his life and ministry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-12/
- JFB: Paul wants people to judge him by what they see him do and hear him teach now, not by past revelations. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html

**v. 7: the thorn (the main point of disagreement)**
- Who gave it? Most writers say God. Sam Storms (charismatic) calls "was given" a "divine passive," meaning God is the hidden actor, and notes the verb normally means God giving a gift. Satan would never aim to keep Paul humble. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/pauls-thorn-in-the-flesh--1---2-cor--12:7-10-
  - Desiring God (Baptist) makes the same argument from the purpose stated twice in the verse: Satan's purpose in this world is not to eliminate conceit in God's people. That's God's purpose. So, God is the one who gave the thorn. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/your-thorn-for-the-shaming-of-satan
- The word "thorn": Guzik says the root word suggests *a tent stake*, not a thumbtack. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-12/
- What was it? Views by tradition:
  - **Unknown:** Guzik lists spiritual harassment, persecution, physical or mental illness, and lustful thoughts, and says we lack the information to decide. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/weekly-devotionals/thorn-in-the-flesh/
  - **Reformed (Calvin, quoted by Storms):** "flesh" here means the unregenerate part of the soul. The thorn covers all of Paul's trials and temptations. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/pauls-thorn-in-the-flesh--1---2-cor--12:7-10-
  - **The Gospel Coalition (Canada):** the writer argues it was an evil spirit God permitted to tempt Paul *in the flesh*, that is, through his desires of the flesh, possibly his pride. https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/detrinitate/what-was-pauls-thorn-in-the-flesh/
  - **Desiring God:** perhaps a physical illness, maybe of the eyes (Gal 4:15), or the super-apostles and false brothers who kept hounding him. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/why-you-have-that-thorn
  - **JFB:** a personal affliction that came after the revelation, with bouts of bodily pain and shame. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html
  - **Storms on other views:** he rejects emotional or psychological explanations such as depression, saying nothing shows it was a recurring problem. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/pauls-thorn-in-the-flesh--1---2-cor--12:7-10-
- **Catholic readings:**
  - Storms reports that Catholic interpreters have mostly followed the Vulgate's *stimulus carnis* ("goad of the flesh") and read it as sexual desire. He rejects this: God would not tell Paul to stop praying about lust, and Paul would not boast in it. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/pauls-thorn-in-the-flesh--1---2-cor--12:7-10-
  - A catholic.com writer, by contrast, concludes it was a visible eye disease, linked to Paul's blinding on the Damascus road. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/tracking-down-pauls-thorn-in-the-flesh

**v. 8**
- Guzik: Paul did what he taught others to do (Phil 4:6). G. Campbell Morgan thought "three times" was a Hebrew way of saying "over and over." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-12/
- JFB and Storms both compare it with Jesus praying three times in Gethsemane. Storms adds that it may mean three flare-ups, or simply repeated prayer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html ; https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/pauls-thorn-in-the-flesh--1---2-cor--12:7-10-

**v. 9**
- JFB: the trial remains, but grace remains too. "Rest on me" literally means "pitch a tent over me," an allusion to God's glory dwelling in the temple. God's way is not to remove his children from trials but to strengthen them to bear them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html
- MacLaren: Christ doesn't promise new grace. He opens Paul's eyes to grace he already has ("is sufficient," not "will be"). https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/2corinthians/strength-in-weakness.cfm
- A commentator quoted on StudyLight says the promise is help to endure suffering, not removal of all suffering. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/12-9.html
- Desiring God: God makes Paul weak so that Christ can be seen to be strong on his behalf. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/our-weakness-reveals-his-worth

**v. 10**
- JFB: "I delight" is better rendered "I am well content." "Weaknesses" is the general term; the other items are examples, some from Satan's messenger and some from people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html
- Matthew Henry calls "when I am weak, then I am strong" a Christian paradox: weak in ourselves, strong in Christ's grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/12-9.html

**v. 11**
- JFB: the "you" is emphatic. The Corinthians should have commended Paul themselves instead of forcing him to commend himself. "I am nothing" means nothing in himself (1 Cor 15:9–10). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html

**v. 12: cessationists and continuationists disagree here**
- **Cessationist (John MacArthur, gty.org):** these signs set apart the true apostles. Miracles faded as the apostles died, and if anybody and everybody could do that, then it wouldn't be the sign of a true apostle. He also notes the passive "were performed": Paul claims no power of his own. https://www.gty.org/sermons/47-85/the-signs-of-an-apostle-part-1
- **JFB:** the signs weren't handed down, and neither was the apostleship. The apostles have no literal successors. Perseverance is the setting the signs happened in, not one of the signs. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html
- **Continuationist (Sam Storms):** grammatically, "signs, wonders and miracles" accompany the marks of an apostle; they are not the marks themselves. Miracles were *necessary* but not *sufficient* proof of apostleship, and non-apostles worked miracles too (1 Cor 12). https://www.samstorms.org/enjoying-god-blog/post/why-do-cessationists-continue-to-cite-2-corinthians-1212-to-defend-their-position

**v. 13**
- JFB: the Corinthians may have taken Paul's refusal of support as a slight, a sign he trusted or loved them less. Hence the ironic "forgive me this wrong." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html
- MacArthur counts this unselfishness as the third sign of Paul's apostleship. https://www.gty.org/sermons/47-85/the-signs-of-an-apostle-part-1

**v. 14**
- JFB: Paul's second visit was probably short and painful. "Third time" means actual visits, not just plans. As their spiritual father, he stores up spiritual treasure for them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html

**v. 15**
- JFB: "spend" means everything he has; "be spent" means everything he is. That goes further than earthly parents do. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html

**v. 16**
- Everyone I found agrees Paul is quoting or mocking his critics' charge. He is not admitting to trickery.
  - Guzik: sarcasm about the claim that Paul would pocket the Jerusalem collection. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-12/
  - The Pulpit Commentary, Gill and Calvin say the same. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/12-16.htm
- **Methodist and Wesleyan writers** stress the moral point. Clarke calls it abominable to use this verse to justify deceit for religious ends. Benson says Paul flatly denies it, so the plea for "holy guile" has no basis. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/12-16.html

**vv. 17–18**
- JFB: Paul's helpers were as unselfish as he was. "Same spirit" means inwardly; "same steps" means outwardly. "Our brother" was probably one of the brothers mentioned in chapter 8. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html
- Benson: no one knows who the brother was. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/12-16.htm

**v. 19**
- JFB follows manuscripts that read "all this time you have thought…" Paul isn't defending himself before them. He speaks before God, for their building up. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html

**v. 20**
- JFB: Paul fears he may have to come as a stern disciplinarian. Terms explained: "rivalry" means self-seeking schemes for gain; "slander" is open, "gossip" is whispered; "arrogance" means puffed-up pride. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html

**v. 21**
- JFB: "my God" shows Paul submitting to God's will. A faithful pastor feels his people's sins as his own humbling. Disregard for pastoral authority tends toward unchecked immorality. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-corinthians-12.html
